title: Physiology and Pathophysiology in Ultra-Marathon Running
population: Overview of the ultra-marathon literature (mostly recreational and age-group ultrarunners)
findings: Ultra-marathoners are older and have a larger weekly training volume, but run more slowly in training, than marathoners.

Previous experience (number of ultra finishes, personal-best marathon time) is the most important predictor of ultra performance, followed by low BMI/body fat and training characteristics (high volume and running speed in training).

The fastest ultra times are generally achieved at 35-45 years or older, and the age of peak performance rises with race distance or duration; the sex difference has fallen to about 10-20% depending on race length.
In longer ultras about 50-60% of participants have musculoskeletal problems, most commonly ankle and knee; creatine kinase can reach 100,000-200,000 U/l depending on fitness and race length.
Ultras are associated with exercise-associated hyponatremia (with heat or cold extremes), digestive problems and temporary biomarker changes that usually normalise after the race.
limitations: Narrative (non-systematic) review by the group whose studies it summarises; no pooled effect sizes; much underlying evidence is cross-sectional. Full text not read.
implications: Use marathon personal best and prior ultra finishes as the primary inputs for 50 km to 100 mile goal-time estimation, ahead of training-derived estimates.
Do not apply an age penalty to ultra goals before about 35-45 years; peak age rises with distance.
Budget a real post-race recovery block after 100 km or longer events; no day count is justified by this review.

verification.notes: Crossref (2018-06-01) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched; all claims stated in the abstract.
